coord_source_note: Hand-worked sea_position nine nautical miles due east of Portland Bill, the wording on the English Wikipedia page HMS Elgin (J39) for the acoustic-mine damage on 4 May 1944. Portland Bill is taken as 50.5144 N, 2.4572 W (existing place PL4183). One nautical mile is 1.852 km, so nine nautical miles are 16.668 km. At latitude 50.5144, one degree of longitude is about 70.816 km (111.32 km times cos 50.5144). 16.668 / 70.816 = 0.2354 degrees, so the point is 50.5144 N, 2.2218 W. Nautical miles are used because the source is a Royal Navy minesweeper at sea. coord_reference_id is left blank because the point is worked, not taken from a single gazetteer.

current_activity: passing from VII Corps to XIX Corps control at noon
notes: Event date: Breakout-15 p296: at noon on 28 July Corlett's XIX Corps assumed responsibility for CCA of the 2nd Armored Division, reinforced by the 4th Division's 22nd Infantry, in the corps' new zone; Breakout-16 p304 says CCA and the 30th Division had been transferred from VII to XIX Corps. Event definition: a combat command of the 2nd Armored Division passes temporarily to XIX Corps while the rest of the division (less CCA) stays under VII Corps; this is a different relationship from the whole-division moves in C0509 and C0511. Relationship: unspecified_subordination to XIX Corps (the text says transferred); organic to the 2nd Armored Division. Review (14 November 2026, Combat Command A later-claims pass): the earlier reading that the end of the temporary arrangement is not documented as a date for CCA, with the whole division under XIX Corps by 2 August (C0226), is superseded. The old reading is that the end was not documented as a date for CCA. The new reading is that Breakout-15 p304 says CCA reverted to 2d Armored Division control on 2 August when Tessy-sur-Vire was secured; the same day, Breakout-23 p449 has the 29th Division, with CCA attached, attacking from the Percy-Tessy line toward Vire. On 6 August CCA on Hill 219 was designated XIX Corps reserve and the rest of the division prepared to move into the VII Corps zone (Breakout-23 p451; Breakout-24 p471: the division less CCA departed the XIX Corps sector shortly after midnight, 6 August). The day CCA rejoined the division is not stated (CCA is with the division at Elbeuf on 25 August, C9449). CR0177 remains open_at_last_claim; last listed is 6 August 1944 (C9448). The 1 August Tessy attack, the 6 August reserve designation, and later actions are in C9447-C9451; the 29th Division attachment is CR1313. The change rests on later pages of the same official history, and later chapters, that date the 29th attachment and the continued XIX Corps split after 28 July. Location: Breakout-15 p296 has CCA in possession of its Cobra objective, Le Mesnil-Herman, and probing toward Villebaudon and Tessy-sur-Vire at noon on 28 July; the point is the village centroid. The 22nd Infantry was attached to CCA. Breakout-15 p302: for the attack of 1 August Corlett attached CCA to the 29th Division, so CCA was still under XIX Corps on 31 July. Commander not verified. Event support: high (Green Book, noon 28 July). Location support: moderate (village named in the text, centroid). current_activity: designated XIX Corps reserve on Hill 219 west of Vire
notes: Event date: 6 August 1944 (Breakout-23 p451). Event definition: Corlett decided it was unprofitable to keep using the 2d Armored Division combat commands to spearhead the infantry attacks; he instructed Brooks to move the division off the roads so the 28th and 29th Divisions could pass through; the armored division, except CCA on Hill 219, now designated XIX Corps reserve, assembled and prepared to move into the VII Corps zone. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). current_activity: Totalize: clears the woods north of Cauvicourt, takes the village and fights in St. Sylvain

I, p. 424: "Polish Armoured Division on the left of the corps front started from Robertmesnil and during the day took St. Sylvain, Cauvicourt, Soignolles". current_activity: Canadian Scottish take Point 168 north of Falaise in a costly afternoon attack; 7th Brigade on Point 159 next day
notes: Event date: 15 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 249). Event definition: On the second day of the advance towards Falaise the 1st Canadian Scottish Regiment, under the 2nd Armoured Brigade, takes Point 168 east of the Falaise road with its heaviest casualties of the campaign so far; on 16 August the 7th Brigade is on the high ground about Point 159 (p. 250). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 249: "On the ridge immediately east of the Falaise Road the 1st Battalion Canadian Scottish Regiment, fighting under command of the 2nd Armoured Brigade, and supported by the 1st Hussars, met and beat down tenacious opposition on Point 168"; p. 250: "Meanwhile the 3rd Division had pushed south from Point 168 and the 7th Brigade occupied the high ground about Point 159"; p. 248: "On the morning of the 15th our advance towards Falaise was resumed". Location: Falaise, Calvados (north of the town) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: Point 168 is a map height a few miles north of Falaise; the point is the town of Falaise and stands for the area, with a wider precision. current_activity: Model takes over Army Group B (and OB West) from Kluge
notes: Event date: Wikipedia's Army Group B page lists Model as commander from 17 August 1944 (Hausser acting 15 to 17 August) and its OB West page lists Model as acting commander from 17 August. The CMH Green Book (Breakout and Pursuit ch. 27 p. 532, 535, row of G018) puts the assumption of command at midnight after 18 August. The sources do not agree and neither is judged better, so both rows are disputed. Event support: the event itself is stated in the cited text (see Event date); only the headquarters place is a representative point. Location support fallback: the point is La Roche-Guyon, the headquarters of claims C0011 and C0202, used as a representative point. Review (German Batch 2 follow-up, 27 October 2026; notes and references only, no value changed): the Lexikon der Wehrmacht (Heeresgruppe B, "Generalfeldmarschall Walter Model 17. August 1944 - Kapitulation") and the Bundesarchiv listing RH 19-IX on the EHRI portal ("17.8.1944: Generalfeldmarschall Walter Model") also date Model's command of Army Group B from 17 August; they are one source family with the Tessin-based Wikipedia list, so the 17 August side of group G018 has one family and the CMH (midnight after 18 August, p. 535) the other. Schramm p. 465 and CMH p. 531 date his arrival at the headquarters to 17 August, a different event from taking over command (see C0933). The group stays disputed with no winner; confidence stays 0.3 because the place is a representative fallback point. Nothing in the dataset says that Model's command ended on 14 September: that date of the old task text is the move to Oosterbeek (see C0934); Army Group B was dissolved on 17 April 1945 (see C0937).

current_activity: with the 21st Panzer Division, pulled back behind the Meurthe; detachments cut off by the French raid to Vathiménil
notes: Event date: night of 19-20 September 1944 (Cole, ch. 4). Event definition: After the 79th Division breaches the Mortagne line on 19 September, the 21st Panzer Division, reinforced by the brigade, is pulled back behind the Meurthe; detachments on the south flank are trapped by the French raid to Vathiménil and flee on foot, abandoning over two hundred vehicles and some tanks of the brigade (Cole, ch. 4). Opponents: US 79th Infantry Division; French 2nd Armored Division.

current_activity: forty-two Panthers attack in fog from Bourdonnay via Ley toward Bezange and run into CCA, 4th Armored Division
notes: Event date: 19 September 1944, from about 0800 (Cole, ch. 5; Wikipedia). Event definition: After a night march from Bourdonnay the brigade, with forty-two Panthers and the 2113th Panzer Grenadier Regiment in the lead, reorganizes near Ley and pushes through heavy fog toward Bezange; in the meeting engagement with CCA it attacks in consecutive jabs and loses heavily (Cole, ch. 5; Wikipedia, Battle of Arracourt). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Location: Bezange-la-Petite, Moselle (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Cole names Bourdonnay, Ley and Bezange. Commander: Colonel Erich Freiherr von Seckendorff (Cole, ch. 5, n. 32; Wikipedia). Opponents: US 4th Armored Division (CCA). Context: The Bezange named by Cole is taken as Bezange-la-Petite, on the road from Ley toward Arracourt (inferred value).

current_activity: Varsity: commands the 6th British and 17th US Airborne Divisions in the drop on the Diersfordter Forst
notes: Event date: 24 March 1945, shortly before 10:00 (CMH, The Last Offensive, ch. 14, p. 309: the airborne armada appears over the Rhine). Event definition: The corps headquarters, attached to the British Second Army for the Rhine crossing, controls the 6th British and 17th US Airborne Divisions, which drop and land north-west of Wesel to seize the high ground of the Diersfordter Forst; General Ridgway and his staff do not take part in the drop but are in position on the west bank of the Rhine (MacDonald, ch. 14, pp. 298-300, 310; Ellis, vol. II, p. 285). After the crossing the corps is relieved of its British units, which pass to the British Second Army, and its headquarters shifts to the US First Army to take command of the units facing the Sieg River in the reduction of the Ruhr Pocket, attacking under First Army on 6 April (MacDonald, ch. 16, pp. 357, 362, 365; the first plan is of 29 March, the shift is read as 2 April, see the relations). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and CMH, MacDonald, The Last Offensive). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 285: "Second Army: XII Corps (Assault)"; "XVIIT U.S. Airborne Corps (Assault): 6th British and 17th U.S. Airborne Divisions"; MacDonald, The Last Offensive, ch. 14, p. 298: "As of 9 March, when Montgomery issued his basic order, plans for using the two airborne divisions that were attached to the Second Army and headquarters of the XVIII Airborne Corps that controlled them still were indefinite"; p. 299: "was to be made by the XVIII Airborne Corps under General Ridgway, employing the British 6th Airborne Division and the U.S. 17th"; p. 300: "to seize high ground crowned by the Diersfordter Forst northwest of Wesel"; p. 309: "shortly before 1000 on 24 March the steady drone of hundreds of aircraft motors began to emerge from the west"; p. 310: "the commander, General Ridgway, and staff of the XVIII Airborne Corps did not participate in the airborne assault but were already in position on the west bank of the Rhine"; ch. 16, p. 357: "British units within the corps passing to the British Second Army"; p. 362: "shifted to the First Army and assumed command of those units facing northward along the Sieg River"; p. 365: "The III Corps began to attack on 5 April, the XVIII Airborne Corps the next day". Location: Diersfordt, North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0437), the village at the Diersfordter Forst, the corps objective with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the objective of the corps (the village of Diersfordt at the Diersfordter Forst), not the position of the corps headquarters, which CMH puts on the west bank of the Rhine (p. 310) without naming a place; the precision is 10 km. Location support: CMH names the Diersfordter Forst north-west of Wesel as the corps objective; Ellis lists the corps and its two divisions for the assault (p. 285). Commander: Maj. Gen. Matthew B. Ridgway, commanding the XVIII Airborne Corps (CMH, The Last Offensive, ch. 14). Context: Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026): the row is the one US claim written in this follow-up. It gives the corps the Second Army as its operational parent for Operation Plunder-Varsity; it is 0.3 because the point is the objective, not the headquarters. The validator gives one expected warning for this row (it is not an error): the row lists the US First Army relation (CR0922, operational_control) with a start of 2 April 1945, after the row date; the row states that start (and the end of the Second Army attachment, CR0921, on 1 April) from MacDonald, ch. 16, pp. 357, 362 and 365, because no other row of the corps exists in April 1945 to state them and the corps would otherwise have no army above it after the Plunder attachment; both dates are inferred values and say so in the relation notes.
